universalAnswers.whatHappened: The House passed H.R. 9340 by 417–3 on September 16; a September 17 Senate unanimous-consent attempt drew an objection, and the separate S.5028 was referred to committee September 18.
universalAnswers.plainLanguageIdentity: A House-passed proposal for state regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider how qualifying large computing customers pay grid-upgrade costs.
universalAnswers.evidenceBasis: House-engrossed bill text, official House roll call and two Senate participant accounts.
universalAnswers.evidenceLimits: No enactment, state adoption, utility rate order or household bill result is established.
universalAnswers.readerRelevance: The proposal addresses whether upgrade costs for very large data-centre loads are allocated to the new customer or potentially spread elsewhere.
universalAnswers.affectedPeople: Covered large-load customers, utilities, state regulators and existing electricity customers whose rates may be affected by local cost allocation.
universalAnswers.changesNow: The bill advanced from the House to the Senate; household rates did not change from that vote.
universalAnswers.uncertainty: Further Senate action, enactment, state determinations, project facts and rate outcomes remain open.
universalAnswers.readerAction: Identify the decision-maker, upgrade, proposed payer and actual legal or rate-case stage.
universalAnswers.betterQuestion: Which authority is deciding who pays for which specific grid upgrade, and what stage has that decision reached?

legal-policy.legalStatus: H.R. 9340 passed the House and was not enacted in the inspected official sources through September 23. A separate Senate bill, S.5028, was referred to committee September 18.
legal-policy.jurisdiction: Federal proposal working through state regulatory authorities and nonregulated utilities under PURPA; actual rates remain utility- and jurisdiction-specific.
legal-policy.parties: The House passed the bill; state regulators and nonregulated utilities would consider it if enacted; Husted sought Senate passage and Heinrich objected.
legal-policy.allegationVsFinding: Vote, text and objection are documented. Promised savings and projected rate effects are advocacy or unresolved outcomes.
legal-policy.currentEffect: Legislative advancement only; no national rate mandate or household-bill change.
legal-policy.unresolvedQuestions: Senate action, enactment, local adoption, covered projects, upgrade costs and actual rate allocation.
legal-policy.nextMilestone: Any further Senate committee or floor action on H.R. 9340 or S.5028, followed by any enactment or local rate proceeding.

translation.newsVersionExact: The U.S. House passed H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, by 417–3 on September 16. That vote did not make the bill law or change a household electricity rate.
translation.actualMeaningExact: The bill would require state utility regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider the standard: begin consideration or set a hearing within one year, then complete it and make a determination within two.
translation.mechanismExact: Whether those upgrade costs reach existing customers depends on local rules, the project and the approved rate design.
translation.familiarExampleExact: For a local claim, ask: which utility or commission is deciding, which upgrade is needed, who would pay under the proposed rate, and whether you are looking at a bill, an enacted rule or an approved rate case.

jargon.plainMeaning: a covered non-residential computing or data facility with peak demand of at least 100 megawatts at one site or campus
